# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

DQL (Dynatrace Query Language) is how you ask Grail anything that the ready-made apps do not show. Like SPL it is a pipeline: fetch reads a data type (logs, spans, events, problems), filter keeps matching records, fields and fieldsAdd shape them, summarize aggregates, sort and limit present the result — and timeseries reads metrics. The same few commands answer most operational questions across logs, traces, metrics and events.  
In this lab you query the easyTravel logs, spans, metrics and events that OneAgent already sends to Grail, observe the checkout failures the instructor creates by switching on the CreditCardCheckError500 fault, and write DQL to find them: error logs by process, failed requests by service and endpoint, failure rates and latency percentiles from spans, service and host metric time series, and a deployment event and Davis problems placed on the same timeline.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You can answer "which service and endpoint fails, since when, how badly" with DQL. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You will query logs, spans, metrics and events with one language and combine the results. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Your queries become Notebook sections the team can reuse during incidents. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

DQL is a pipeline of commands. Every query starts with a data source command and is refined with \|.  
*Figure: DQL Pipeline — fetch logs \| spans \| events \| dt.davis.problems  (or timeseries for metrics) \| filter \| fields / fieldsAdd \| summarize … by: {…} \| sort \| limit*

| Command | Purpose | Example | SPL Equivalent |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| fetch | Read a data type with an optional time range | fetch logs, from: now() \- 30m | index=… earliest=-30m |
| filter / fields / fieldsAdd | Keep matching records; choose or calculate fields | filter loglevel \== "ERROR" \| fields timestamp, content | search / where · table · eval |
| summarize / makeTimeseries | Aggregate (by groups / over time) | summarize n \= count(), by: {service.name} | stats … by · timechart |
| timeseries / sort / limit | Metrics as series; order; cut | timeseries avg(dt.host.cpu.usage) | mstats · sort · head |

*Figure: Four Data Types, One Language — logs (content, loglevel) · spans (duration, request.is\_failed, span.name) · metrics (timeseries) · events / problems (event.type, event.status)*

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

* Explain the DQL pipeline: fetch, filter, fields, summarize, sort, limit  
* Query logs in Grail to find application errors  
* Write DQL on spans to identify failing services and endpoints, failure rates and latency percentiles  
* Discover and query metrics with metrics and timeseries  
* Send and query a deployment event; query Davis problems  
* Combine the results into an evidence-based failure analysis

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Reading Records vs Reading Metrics

fetch reads records — individual log lines, spans, events, problems — that you can filter field by field and aggregate with summarize (or makeTimeseries for a chart). Metrics are already aggregated time series and are read with timeseries, which takes an aggregation (avg, sum, max, percentile …), optional by: dimensions and filters, and returns one array of values per series. Choosing the right starting command is the first decision in every DQL query.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| A Notebook with five good DQL sections — errors by service, failed endpoints, p95 by service, a key metric, recent events — is an incident starter kit. |
|  |
| Because logs, spans, metrics and events share fields such as service.name, dt.entity.host and trace IDs, one language can follow an incident across all of them. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: filter vs summarize Order

DQL processes commands in order. filter before summarize reduces the records that are aggregated (fast and correct for "errors per service"); filter after summarize works on the aggregated rows (for example keep only services with more than 10 errors). Putting a record-level condition after summarize fails because the field no longer exists — exactly like where after stats in SPL.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With DQL |
| :---- |
| A query like fetch logs \| summarize count(), by: {service.name} \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" returns nothing, and the user concludes there are no errors. |
|  |
| REASON: After summarize only service.name and the count exist; loglevel is gone, so the filter matches nothing. |
|  |
| YOU MUST filter records first, then summarize; inspect fields with \| limit 5 before writing filters on unfamiliar data. |

## 3.3  DQL Building Blocks Used in This Lab

| Need | DQL | Data Type | Note |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Text match | filter matchesPhrase(content, "Connection is not available") | logs | Phrase search on the log text |
| Failure rate | summarize total \= count(), failed \= countIf(request.is\_failed \== true) | spans | fieldsAdd rate \= 100.0 \* failed / total |
| Percentile | summarize p95 \= percentile(duration, 95), by: {service.name} | spans | duration is a duration value |
| Metric discovery | metrics \| filter startsWith(metric.key, "dt.service.request") | metrics | Find exact metric keys before timeseries |

| 📝  How to Decide Which Data Type to Fetch |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Do I need individual records or a pre-aggregated trend?" For messages and exceptions, fetch logs. For which request failed or was slow, fetch spans. For resource and long-term trends, use timeseries on metrics. For what changed or what Davis detected, fetch events or dt.davis.problems. Then filter early and summarize late. |

| TASK 1 — LOGS: fetch, filter, fields, sort, summarize |
| :---- |

| 1 | Query Logs in Grail to Find Application Errors*Dynatrace Grail & DQL SOP — Day 3 — Lab 3* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

Your instructor records the "deployment" as an event and switches on the CreditCardCheckError500 fault; you confirm the data is arriving and then build log queries step by step in a new Notebook: raw records, a filtered and shaped list, counts per process, and a phrase search.

| ⌨  Task 1 — Instructor Cues and Data Check |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Step 1: Instructor cue — easyTravel and OneAgent are already running; you do nothing on the host |
| \# Wait for the announcement: "Deploy easyTravel Checkout Service v2.4.1 recorded — CreditCardCheckError500 fault ON at HH:MM". Write that time down. |
|  |
| \# Step 2: Confirm the data is arriving — add a Notebook section and run: |
| fetch logs, from: now() \- 10m \| summarize count(), by: {[dt.process.name](http://dt.process.name)} ![][image4] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: the instructor's announcement with the fault start time (HH:MM) |
| Step 2: rows for the easyTravel processes; counts grow every minute |

| ⌨  Task 1 — Notebook: new section per query (wait 2–3 minutes after the fault) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Q1 — what does an easyTravel log record look like? |
| fetch logs, from: now() \- 15m \| filter contains(content, "CreditCardCheckError500") \| limit 3 |
| ![][image5] |
| \# Q2 — error records, chosen fields, newest first |
| fetch logs, from: now() \- 15m |
| \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" |
| \| fields timestamp, dt.process.name, loglevel, content |
| \| sort timestamp desc \| limit 10 |
| ![][image6] |
| \# Q3 — errors per process |
| fetch logs, from: now() \- 15m \| filter loglevel \== "ERROR" \| summarize errors \= count(), by: {dt.process.name} \| sort errors desc |
| ![][image7] |
| \# Q4 — phrase search: which processes report the credit-card fault? |
| fetch logs, from: now() \- 15m \| filter contains(content, "CreditCardCheckError500") \| summarize count(), by: {[dt.process.name](http://dt.process.name)} ![][image8] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Q1: records with timestamp, content, loglevel, dt.process.name, log.source … (inspect the field names; one line mentions CreditCardCheckError500) |
| Q2: ERROR lines from the easyTravel backend whose content mentions the credit-card check and CreditCardCheckError500, newest first |
| Q3: the process that runs the easyTravel backend has the highest error count; other processes have few or none |
| Q4: the same backend process only — the fault text is logged in one place |
| **1.A  Record the Q3 counts. Which process has most of the errors, and why?**  Answer: The backend process has by far the most errors because the CreditCardCheckError500 fault is raised inside the easyTravel backend's credit-card check. Other processes log few or no errors, so the error count points to the backend process as the source rather than the frontend that only passes the request on. |
| **1.B  Write Q3 in SPL for the Splunk d3\_app index (Day 3 Lab 1). Which DQL command corresponds to stats … by?** Answer:  index=d3\_app level=ERROR \| stats count AS errors BY service \| sort \- errors The DQL command `summarize` corresponds to Splunk's `stats ... by`. |

| TASK 2 — SPANS: Identify Application Failures |
| :---- |

| 2 | Write DQL Queries on Spans to Identify Failing Services, Endpoints and LatencyDynatrace Grail & DQL SOP — Day 3 — Lab 3 | ⏱ 8 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

Spans tell you which requests failed and how long they took. You count failed requests by service and endpoint, calculate a failure rate with countIf and fieldsAdd, compare latency percentiles, and draw failures over time with makeTimeseries.

| ⌨  Task 2 — Notebook sections |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Q5 — failed requests by service and endpoint (span name) |
| fetch spans, from: now() \- 15m |
| \| filter request.is\_failed \== true |
| \| summarize failed \= count(), by: {service.name, span.name} \| sort failed desc |
| ![][image9] |
| \# Q6 — failure rate per service and endpoint (only endpoints with failures) |
| fetch spans, from: now() \- 15m |
| \| summarize total \= count(), failed \= countIf(request.is\_failed \== true), by: {service.name, span.name} \| filter failed \> 0 |
| \| fieldsAdd failure\_rate \= round(100.0 \* failed / total, decimals: 1\) \| sort failure\_rate desc \| limit 10 |
| ![][image10] |
| \# Q7 — latency percentiles by service |
| fetch spans, from: now() \- 15m |
| \| summarize p50 \= percentile(duration, 50), p95 \= percentile(duration, 95), by: {service.name} \| sort p95 desc |
| ![][image11] |
| \# Q8 — failures per minute, all services (chart) |
| fetch spans, from: now() \- 30m |
| \| makeTimeseries failed \= countIf(request.is\_failed \== true), interval: 1m  ![][image12] |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Q5: one or two easyTravel services with failed requests; the top row is the request (span name) behind the credit-card check or booking — write down its service and span name |
| Q6: the booking / credit-card request shows a clearly non-zero failure rate; ordinary page and search requests are at or near 0 % (they are not listed because of filter failed \> 0 if they never failed) |
| Q7: p95 per service; the failing backend service is not necessarily the slowest — error responses return quickly |
| Q8: zero or near zero before the fault start time, then failures every minute until the instructor switches the fault off |
| **2.A  Paste Q6. Which request fails and at what rate? Why do other requests of the same application not fail?**  Answer: The credit-card / booking request of the easyTravel backend (the span name at the top of Q6) fails at a clearly non-zero rate during the fault. Other requests such as page views and searches do not fail because CreditCardCheckError500 is raised only inside the credit-card check, which only the booking step calls. |
| **2.B  If request.is\_failed returns nothing in your tenant, how would you find the right field (hint: Q1 approach on spans)?**  Answer: Run fetch spans, from: now() \- 15m \| limit 5 to inspect sample span records and their fields. Identify the field that marks failures (for example request.is\_failed, span.status\_code or an http status field) and use it in the filter and aggregation. |

| ⚠️  STOP CHECK — Keep the Fault On for the Metrics Task |
| :---- |

| If in doubt — show your instructor Q5 and Q6 before proceeding to Task 3\. |

| TASK 3 — METRICS: Discover and Query with timeseries |
| :---- |

| 3 | Query Metrics in Grail with metrics and timeseries*Dynatrace Grail & DQL SOP — Day 3 — Lab 3* | ⏱ 6 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

Metrics are read with timeseries. OneAgent provides ready-made service and host metrics, so you first discover the exact keys with the metrics command, then chart service failures, response time and host CPU, and finally watch the series recover when the instructor switches the fault off.

| ⌨  Task 3 — Notebook sections |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Q9 — which service request metrics exist? |
| metrics \| filter startsWith(metric.key, "dt.service.request") \| fields metric.key \| limit 20 |
| ![][image13] |
| \# Q10 — failed requests and response time per service |
| timeseries failures \= sum(dt.service.request.failure\_count),           response \= avg(dt.service.request.response\_time),           by: {dt.entity.service},           from: now() \- 30m \| fieldsAdd service \= getNodeName(dt.entity.service) |
| ![][image14] |
| \# Q11 — host CPU from OneAgent, by host |
| timeseries cpu \= avg(dt.host.cpu.usage),     by: {dt.entity.host},     from: now() \- 30m \| fieldsAdd host \= getNodeName(dt.entity.host) |
| ![][image15] |
| \# Step: when the instructor announces "fault OFF", write the time down and re-run Q10 after 2 minutes |
| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Q9: dt.service.request.count, dt.service.request.failure\_count, dt.service.request.response\_time … (use the keys exactly as listed) |
|  |
| Q10: failures \> 0 for the easyTravel backend service while the fault is ON; after "fault OFF" the failure series falls back to 0; response time stays in the normal range |
| Q11: ip-172-30-0-220, CPU well below saturation — the failures are application errors, not a CPU shortage |
| **3.A  Which signals (Day 1: RED and USE) do Q10 and Q11 represent? What do they prove together?**  Answer: Q10 shows the Rate and Errors signals (and Duration) of the backend service: failures appear while response time stays normal. Q11 shows the Utilization of the host CPU. Together they prove the failures are caused by the application fault, not by resource saturation. |
| **3.B  Why can you use dt.service.request.\* directly, while a custom metric needs an ingest pipeline first?**  Answer: OneAgent detects services automatically and sends the dt.service.request.\* metrics with entity dimensions out of the box, so no configuration or token is needed. A custom metric would first have to be defined and ingested, and then its exact key and dimensions would have to be discovered with the metrics command. |

| **4.A  Write the failure story with times from Q12, Q14 and Q10: change → mechanism → symptom → recovery.**  Answer: The Checkout Service v2.4.1 rollout was recorded as a deployment event. Shortly afterwards the CreditCardCheckError500 fault was switched on. The backend started returning HTTP 500 from the credit-card check, shown by the ERROR logs, the failed spans and the rising failure count. When the instructor switched the fault off, the failures stopped and Davis closed the problem.   |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Q1 returns no records | The instructor has not switched on the fault yet, or the time range is too short | Check the instructor's cue time; widen from: now() \- 30m | Wait for the cue; tell your instructor if still empty after 3 minutes |
| Q1 shows other field names | Different log attribute mapping | Inspect a record | Adapt filters (e.g. status vs loglevel) to your fields |
| Q5 empty although errors exist | request.is\_failed not set on these spans | fetch spans, from: now() \- 15m \| limit 3 | Use the error field you find (e.g. span status) in the filter |
| Q9 lists no service metrics | OneAgent not reporting or wrong timeframe | metrics \| limit 20 | Tell your instructor; re-run Q9 after 2 minutes |
| timeseries: unknown metric key | Key has a suffix (e.g. .gauge) | Run Q9 again | Copy the key exactly from Q9 |
| Q12 empty | Event stored as Davis event or not linked to an entity | fetch dt.davis.events \| filter event.type \== "CUSTOM\_DEPLOYMENT" | Query dt.davis.events; ask your instructor whether the deployment event was posted |

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — DQL vs SPL |
| :---- |
| Without notes: translate fetch \| filter \| summarize \| sort into SPL. |
| What is the DQL equivalent of timechart? |
|  |
| Key answer to explore: index/search \| where \| stats \| sort; makeTimeseries (records) or timeseries (metrics). |
| **Discussion 2 — Records vs Metrics** |
| When did you use fetch and when timeseries? Could you have answered Q10 from logs? |
| Which is cheaper to keep for months? |
|  |
| Key insight: metrics are compact and fast for trends; records give detail for investigation. |
| **Discussion 3 — Discover Before You Query** |
| Why did Q1 and Q9 come before the "real" queries? |
| What goes wrong when you guess field names or metric keys? |
|  |
| Key answer: inspecting data first prevents empty results and wrong conclusions. |
| **Discussion 4 — Events Make the Story** |
| How did the deployment event change the conclusion of your analysis? |
| Who should send deployment events automatically? |
|  |
| Answer: a change just before the failures is the first root-cause candidate; CI/CD pipelines should send events for every deployment. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Filter after summarize on record fields | SQL habits | Empty results | Filter records first |
| No from: in fetch | Default range assumed | Too much or too little data | Always set from: now() \- \<window\> |
| Guessing metric keys | Names look obvious | "unknown metric" errors | Discover with metrics \| filter … |
| Cumulative OTel metrics | SDK defaults | Metrics not ingested | Delta temporality (cumulativetodelta) |
| Ignoring events | Focus on errors | Change-related cause missed | Query events next to failures |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — DYNATRACE GRAIL & DQL COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Records | fetch logs \| spans \| events \| dt.davis.problems, from: now() \- 30m | Data source |
| Filter | \| filter service.name \== "x" and loglevel \== "ERROR" | Keep records |
| Phrase | \| filter matchesPhrase(content, "…") | Log text |
| Shape | \| fields a, b · \| fieldsAdd c \= … | Choose / calculate |
| Aggregate | \| summarize n \= count(), by: {service.name} | Group |
| Conditional count | countIf(request.is\_failed \== true) | Failures |
| Percentile | percentile(duration, 95\) | Latency |
| Chart records | \| makeTimeseries count(), interval: 1m | Records over time |
| Metrics | timeseries avg(dt.host.cpu.usage), by: {dt.entity.host} | Metric series |
| Find keys | metrics \| filter startsWith(metric.key, "dt.service.request") | Discovery |
| Order / cut | \| sort x desc \| limit 10 | Present |
| Events | fetch events \| filter event.type \== "CUSTOM\_DEPLOYMENT" | Changes |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — learners never run these commands. Do this on the easyTravel EC2 host ip-172-30-0-220 (SSH as the instructor) and in the Dynatrace tenant. easyTravel and OneAgent are the same ones used in Day 2 Labs 6–7.  
1\. At least 30 minutes before class, check easyTravel is up and OneAgent is reporting: Dynatrace → Services shows the easyTravel services; Notebook query fetch logs, from: now() \- 10m \| summarize count(), by: {dt.process.name} returns the easyTravel processes. Give learners read access to Notebooks and the ability to create their own u\<seat\>\_ Notebooks only.  
2\. At cue T+0, post the deployment event and switch the CreditCardCheckError500 fault on, then announce the time to the class. Use a token with the events.ingest scope held in your shell only — never in guides, Notebooks or screenshots.

| ⌨  Instructor — Record Deployment, Fault ON (cue T+0) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# Placeholders: DT\_ENV\_URL=https\://\<env-id\>.live.dynatrace.com  DT\_API\_TOKEN=\<token with events.ingest\> |
| curl \-sS \-X POST "\$DT\_ENV\_URL/api/v2/events/ingest" \-H "Authorization: Api-Token \$DT\_API\_TOKEN" \-H "Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8" \-d '{"eventType":"CUSTOM\_DEPLOYMENT","title":"easyTravel Checkout Service v2.4.1 Rollout","entitySelector":"type(HOST),entityName.equals(\\"ip-172-30-0-220\\")","properties":{"deployment.name":"easyTravel Checkout Service v2.4.1 Rollout","deployment.version":"v2.4.1","source":"instructor-runbook"}}' |
| curl \-s "http\://localhost:8091/services/ConfigurationService/setPluginEnabled?name=CreditCardCheckError500\&enabled=true"; date \+%T |

3\. Fault timeline for this lab: T+0 deployment event and fault ON (announce HH:MM) → the fault stays ON through Task 3, Q10 → at about T+34 minutes announce "fault OFF" and run the command below → learners re-run Q10 two minutes later. Switch the fault on about 20 minutes before class if you want a Davis problem to exist for Q13.

| ⌨  Instructor — Fault OFF (cue T+34) |
| :---- |
|  |
| curl \-s "http\://localhost:8091/services/ConfigurationService/setPluginEnabled?name=CreditCardCheckError500\&enabled=false"; date \+%T |

4\. At the end of the lab confirm the fault is off (a Notebook query for CreditCardCheckError500 lines shows no new lines after the cue). The same easyTravel host is reused in Day 3 Labs 4–5 with Datadog.
